quickrefs.title: PONV prophylaxis and rescue
quickrefs.summary: How many prophylactic interventions by risk, which agents at what dose and when, and what to give when prophylaxis fails — the Fifth consensus guideline (2025), with the adult dose table as set out in the Fourth (2020).

sections.heading: Adults: risk and how many interventions

Propofol TIVA, avoiding volatile agents and nitrous oxide, regional anesthesia, opioid minimization, adequate hydration, sugammadex rather than neostigmine

sections.note: Doses and timing as tabulated in the Fourth consensus (Gan TJ, et al. Anesth Analg 2020;131:411–448, Table 4); a dash means the table gave no timing. Metoclopramide is no longer recommended for prophylaxis in the Fifth consensus.

sections.heading: Rescue when prophylaxis fails
items: Give an antiemetic from a class that was not used for prophylaxis; repeating the same class within 6 hours adds no benefit.
After 6 hours, a second dose of a 5-HT₃ antagonist or a butyrophenone may be considered when no alternative is available.
Do not re-dose long-acting agents (aprepitant, fosaprepitant, palonosetron) in the PACU.
Amisulpride 10 mg IV was more effective than 5 mg for treatment after failed non-dopaminergic prophylaxis; propofol 20–40 mg is effective as treatment.

sections.heading: How to read it
rows: A at risk · B progressive · C1 asymptomatic severe, ventricle compensated · C2 asymptomatic severe, ventricle decompensated · D symptomatic severe. Symptoms plus stage, not anatomy alone, drive the recommendations.
1 recommended · 2a reasonable · 2b may be considered · 3 no benefit or harm. Level of evidence in brackets: A, B-R, B-NR, C-LD, C-EO.

Low: STS predicted mortality < 3% for AVR (< 1% for mitral repair), no frailty, no major organ compromise, no procedure-specific impediment. High: STS > 8%, ≥ 2 frailty indices, or 1–2 uncorrectable organ systems. Prohibitive: predicted 1-year death or major morbidity > 50%, ≥ 3 organ systems, or a severe impediment.

Severe valve disease is evaluated by a multidisciplinary team when intervention is considered (Class 1); TEER, PMBC, the Ross procedure, bicuspid-root surgery and TAVI for bicuspid valves are tied to a Comprehensive Valve Center.

quickrefs.title: Neuraxial and deep blocks with antithrombotic drugs (ASRA)
quickrefs.summary: How long to wait after each antithrombotic before a neuraxial or deep plexus block, whether a catheter may stay, and when the next dose may follow — the fifth edition (2025), which now writes doses as low or high and extends every interval to deep plexus and deep peripheral blocks.

source.title: Regional Anesthesia in the Patient Receiving Antithrombotic or Thrombolytic Therapy: ASRA Pain Medicine Evidence-Based Guidelines (Fifth Edition)
source.citation: Kopp SL, Vandermeulen E, McBane RD, Perlas A, Leffert L, Horlocker T. Regional anesthesia in the patient receiving antithrombotic or thrombolytic therapy: American Society of Regional Anesthesia and Pain Medicine evidence-based guidelines (fifth edition). Reg Anesth Pain Med. 2025; published online first. doi:10.1136/rapm-2024-105766

sections.heading: Ground rules
items: Every interval below applies to neuraxial blocks and to deep plexus or deep peripheral blocks alike; for other peripheral blocks, judge by the site's compressibility, vascularity and the consequences of bleeding.
Low dose and high dose replace the old prophylactic and therapeutic labels; recommendations are graded strong or conditional.

Review the chart daily for every other hemostasis-altering drug: the additive effect of combinations is the recurring theme. With an indwelling catheter on LMWH, no concomitant antiplatelet drugs, heparin or oral anticoagulants.
Do not use PT/INR or aPTT to judge a DOAC. A drug-calibrated level below 30 ng/mL, or an anti-Xa at or below 0.1 IU/mL, counts as no relevant effect and permits a block before the full hold.
Routine reversal (idarucizumab, andexanet alfa, PCC) just to permit a block is discouraged: wait out the interval instead.
A bloody or difficult placement does not mandate cancelling surgery; with intraoperative heparin, discuss it with the surgeon; with LMWH, delay the first postoperative dose to 24 hours.
Check a platelet count before a neuraxial technique after more than 4 days of heparin or LMWH.

sections.heading: Special situations
items: Obstetrics: the same intervals apply to parturients; exceptions may be appropriate for a high-risk parturient needing urgent intervention when general anesthesia carries the greater risk; converting LMWH to unfractionated heparin near delivery is worth considering.
Warfarin epidurals: routine sensory and motor testing with low-concentration solutions while the catheter is in, and continued checks for 48 hours after removal.
Kidney function and age lengthen the DOAC, fondaparinux and LMWH intervals above; patients with low creatinine clearance are at particular risk.
ASRA's own ASRA Coags app carries the full fifth-edition logic; the full text (RAPM 2025) is the authority when this card and your judgement differ.

quickrefs.title: Valve disease severity by echo (ASE)
quickrefs.summary: The grading tables for native valve stenosis and regurgitation, transcribed from the 2017 EACVI/ASE aortic stenosis update, the 2017 ASE native regurgitation recommendations (Tables 8, 11, 14 and 16) and ASE's 2023 rheumatic heart disease document for mitral and tricuspid stenosis. Grades are mild, moderate and severe; the reading integrates specific, supportive and quantitative signs and discards outliers.

source.title: Recommendations for Noninvasive Evaluation of Native Valvular Regurgitation (ASE 2017); Recommendations on the Echocardiographic Assessment of Aortic Valve Stenosis: A Focused Update (EACVI/ASE 2017); Recommendations for the Use of Echocardiography in the Evaluation of Rheumatic Heart Disease (ASE 2023)
source.citation: Zoghbi WA, et al. J Am Soc Echocardiogr. 2017;30:303–371 (doi:10.1016/j.echo.2017.01.007) · Baumgartner H, et al. J Am Soc Echocardiogr. 2017;30:372–392 (doi:10.1016/j.echo.2017.02.009) · Pandian NG, et al. J Am Soc Echocardiogr. 2023;36:3–28 (doi:10.1016/j.echo.2022.10.009)

sections.heading: Aortic stenosis (EACVI/ASE 2017)
sections.note: Velocity ≥ 4 m/s with a mean gradient ≥ 40 mmHg defines high-gradient AS; below both, low-gradient. A calculated AVA under 1.0 cm² suggests but does not confirm severe AS: a valve producing 40 mmHg at normal flow is nearer 0.8 than 1.0 cm². Average at least 5 beats in irregular rhythm; measure the LVOT at the level of the velocity sample; pressure recovery matters when the ascending aorta is under 30 mm.

sections.heading: Aortic stenosis: low-gradient states
rows: Stroke volume index < 35 mL/m² (normal ≥ 35; high flow > 58)

AVA < 1.0 cm², mean gradient < 40 mmHg, LVEF < 50%, SVi < 35 mL/m² → low-dose dobutamine echo: severe if velocity reaches ≥ 4 m/s or mean gradient > 30–40 mmHg while AVA stays ≤ 1.0 cm² at any flow; an AVA rising above 1.0 cm² means not severe; a > 20% rise in stroke volume shows contractile reserve
AVA < 1.0 cm², velocity < 4 m/s, mean gradient < 40 mmHg, LVEF ≥ 50%, SVi < 35 mL/m² (measured normotensive) → confirm low flow by another technique and apply the likelihood criteria below
SVi ≥ 35 mL/m² with AVA < 1.0 cm²: severe AS is very unlikely; do not label it severe
Likelihood of severe AS when AVA < 1.0 and gradient < 40 with preserved EF

Examination consistent with severe AS; typical symptoms without other explanation; age over 70; LVH; reduced longitudinal LV function without other cause; mean gradient 30–40 mmHg when normotensive; AVA ≤ 0.8 cm²; low flow confirmed by 3D TEE, CT or CMR; CT calcium score severe AS likely at ≥ 2,000 AU in men / ≥ 1,200 in women, very likely ≥ 3,000 / ≥ 1,600, unlikely < 1,600 / < 800
Peak velocity > 5.5 m/s in asymptomatic patients

sections.heading: Aortic regurgitation (ASE 2017, Table 11)
rows: Usually dilated (specific with normal LV function and no other volume load; not in acute AR)
Jet width in LVOT, color flow
Large in central jets; variable in eccentric jets
Diastolic flow reversal in descending aorta, PW
Jet width / LVOT width, central jets (%)
Jet CSA / LVOT CSA, central jets (%)
sections.note: Color Doppler at a Nyquist limit of 50–70 cm/s. PHT shortens with rising LV diastolic pressure and may lengthen in chronic adaptation to severe AR. Quantitative parameters subclassify the moderate group.

sections.heading: Mitral regurgitation (ASE 2017, Table 8)
rows: None or mild leaflet abnormality (mild thickening, calcification or prolapse, mild tenting)
Moderate leaflet abnormality or moderate tenting
Severe valve lesions (primary: flail leaflet, ruptured papillary muscle, severe retraction, large perforation; secondary: severe tenting, poor leaflet coaptation)
Dilated (can be normal in acute severe MR, small patients, or a small LV before the MR)
Large central jet (> 50% of LA) or eccentric wall-impinging jet of variable size
Not visible, transient or small (< 0.3 cm)
Large throughout systole (≥ 1 cm at Nyquist 30–40 cm/s)
Systolic dominance (may be blunted in LV dysfunction or AF)
Minimal to no systolic flow, or systolic flow reversal
≥ 0.40 (may be lower in secondary MR with an elliptical orifice)
sections.note: Nyquist 50–70 cm/s for jets. Inflow and pulmonary-vein signs are influenced by LV diastolic function, AF and LA pressure; the inflow sign is most valid over 50 years. Quantitative parameters subclassify moderate MR (grades II and III); discrepancies among EROA, RVol and RF arise in low- or high-flow states.

sections.heading: Integrating the MR signs (ASE 2017, Figure 18)
rows: Small, narrow central jet · vena contracta ≤ 0.3 cm · PISA radius absent or ≤ 0.3 cm at Nyquist 30–40 cm/s · A-wave dominant inflow · soft or incomplete CW jet · normal LV and LA size
Flail leaflet · vena contracta ≥ 0.7 cm · PISA radius ≥ 1.0 cm at Nyquist 30–40 cm/s · central jet > 50% of LA area · pulmonary-vein systolic flow reversal · enlarged LV with normal function
Two or three, or mixed signals

Quantify: EROA < 0.2 / 0.2–0.29 / 0.30–0.39 / ≥ 0.4 cm², RVol < 30 / 30–44 / 45–59 / ≥ 60 mL, RF < 30 / 30–39 / 40–49 / ≥ 50% = grades I–IV; grade III with three specific signs of severe MR, or an elliptical orifice, is read as severe
Poor image quality, low confidence in the Doppler data, or discordant quantitative, qualitative or clinical findings: TEE or CMR for quantitation
Eccentric wall-impinging jets are underestimated (quantify); single-frame PISA and vena contracta overestimate non-holosystolic MR; RVol for severe MR may be lower in low-flow states
sections.note: Secondary MR: the orifice is crescentic and 2D PISA underestimates it, the EROA is often biphasic, a high E velocity and pulmonary-vein blunting are not specific; 3D vena contracta area can rescue the grade. In the operating room, reduced load or contractility usually underestimates the grade: let the preoperative study guide the decision.

sections.heading: Mitral stenosis (ASE 2023, rheumatic)
sections.note: Planimetry (3D preferred) is the anatomic method; MVA = 220 / pressure half-time; continuity and PISA are reserved for inconclusive cases. Gradients depend on flow and heart rate — report the rhythm and rate and never grade on gradient alone. Pressure half-time misleads with severe AR, immediately after balloon commissurotomy, and with altered LA or LV compliance; trace the mid-diastolic slope of a biphasic E wave. Exercise PA systolic pressure > 60 mmHg marks hemodynamically significant MS.

sections.heading: Tricuspid regurgitation (ASE 2017, Table 14)
rows: Severe valve lesions (flail leaflet, severe retraction, large perforation)
Usually dilated (can be normal in acute severe TR)
Large central jet or eccentric wall-impinging jet of variable size; > 10 cm² at Nyquist > 50–70 cm/s
sections.note: Hepatic-vein and inflow signs are nonspecific (RV diastolic function, AF, RA pressure). Annular dilation: end-diastolic diameter ≥ 40 mm or > 21 mm/m² in the apical four-chamber view (ASE 2023). The massive and torrential grades proposed for transcatheter trials are not ASE grades.

sections.heading: Tricuspid stenosis (ASE 2023)
rows: Mean gradient ≥ 5 mmHg · inflow VTI ≥ 60 cm · valve area by continuity ≤ 1.0 cm² · pressure half-time ≥ 190 ms (less reliable than in MS)
Dilated RA, IVC plethora, septal bowing toward the LA, loss of systolic predominance in hepatic or SVC flow (S/D < 1), tricuspid E/e' > 6
Average 5 or more beats across the respiratory cycle or record at end-expiration; rate preferably 70–80 bpm; valve area is underestimated with more than mild TR

sections.heading: Pulmonic regurgitation (ASE 2017, Table 16)
rows: Thin, usually < 10 mm long, narrow origin
Broad origin; variable depth of penetration; jet width / pulmonary annulus > 0.7
Dense; early termination of diastolic flow; deceleration time < 260 ms; pressure half-time < 100 ms (unreliable with high RV end-diastolic pressure; a steep deceleration is not specific)
Diastolic flow reversal in main or branch PAs, PW
Pulmonic systolic VTI versus LVOT VTI, PW
sections.note: Significant PR is uncommon and usually secondary to pulmonary hypertension or congenital heart disease; combine color, pulsed-wave and CW signs. CMR is the best method to quantify PR and follow RV remodeling.

sections.heading: How ASE grades, and the traps
items: Three grades (mild, moderate, severe; 'trace' when barely detected); integrate every available sign and set aside the outliers rather than averaging them.

Specific signs settle the grade (a vena contracta ≥ 0.7 cm, pulmonary-vein systolic reversal, a flail leaflet); supportive signs (chamber dilation, E velocity, jet density) raise or lower confidence; quantitative EROA, volume and fraction decide the ambiguous middle.
Color settings: Nyquist 50–70 cm/s for jets, aliasing velocity 30–40 cm/s shifted toward the jet for PISA; measure the vena contracta zoomed and perpendicular to the jet.

Jet area is imprecise, especially for eccentric wall-hugging jets; PISA fails with multiple, eccentric or crescentic orifices (the radius error is squared); the vena contracta is unreliable with multiple jets.
Formulas: EROA = 2πr²·Va ÷ peak jet velocity; regurgitant volume = EROA × jet VTI; regurgitant fraction = regurgitant volume ÷ total stroke volume; stroke volume = 0.785·d²·VTI.

quickrefs.title: Local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST)
quickrefs.summary: Recognize it, stop the drug, start lipid at the first serious sign, and run a modified ACLS — the ASRA checklist (2020 version), with the Society for Pediatric Anesthesia's pediatric lipid regimen.

source.title: American Society of Regional Anesthesia and Pain Medicine Checklist for Managing Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity: 2020 Version
source.citation: Neal JM, Neal EJ, Weinberg GL. American Society of Regional Anesthesia and Pain Medicine checklist for managing local anesthetic systemic toxicity: 2020 version. Reg Anesth Pain Med. 2021;46:81–82. doi:10.1136/rapm-2020-101986

sections.heading: Recognize it
items: Think of LAST in any patient with altered mental status, neurologic symptoms or cardiovascular instability after a regional anesthetic — the classic prodrome (metallic taste, perioral numbness, tinnitus, agitation) appears in fewer than half, and sedation hides it.

Central nervous system: excitation then depression, seizures, coma. Cardiovascular: an early hyperdynamic phase, then hypotension, conduction block, bradycardia, ventricular arrhythmias, asystole; cardiovascular signs may be the only ones.
Onset can be delayed 30 minutes or more after injection; keep monitoring after any block.

sections.heading: Immediate steps
items: Stop injecting the local anesthetic.
Call for help and send for the LAST rescue kit; alert the nearest cardiopulmonary bypass or ECMO team now, so support is ready if CPR and lipid fail.
Manage the airway: ventilate with 100% oxygen, avoid hyperventilation (alkalosis and hypocarbia worsen toxicity), secure the airway if needed.

Control seizures with a benzodiazepine; avoid large doses of propofol, above all with hemodynamic instability (small doses are acceptable when stable); low-dose neuromuscular blockade if seizures persist.
Give 20% lipid emulsion at the first sign of a serious event (see the doses below); do not wait for arrest.
If pulseless, CPR with the modified ACLS below; continue lipid and consider extracorporeal support if there is no response.

sections.heading: Lipid emulsion 20%
rows: Bolus 100 mL over 2–3 minutes, then 200–250 mL over 15–20 minutes
Bolus 1.5 mL/kg (lean body weight) over 2–3 minutes, then about 0.25 mL/kg/min
Re-bolus once or twice at the same dose and double the infusion to 0.5 mL/kg/min
At least 10 minutes after circulatory stability; maximum about 12 mL/kg (ideal body weight) — a prolonged resuscitation can approach a litre
Bolus 1.5 mL/kg over 1 minute, infusion 0.25 mL/kg/min, repeat the bolus every 3–5 minutes to 4.5 mL/kg, double the rate if pressure stays low; maximum 10 mL/kg in the first 30 minutes

sections.heading: ACLS modifications
items: Epinephrine in small boluses of 1 mcg/kg or less.
Avoid vasopressin, calcium channel blockers, beta blockers and any further local anesthetic (no lidocaine for arrhythmias); amiodarone is first-line for ventricular arrhythmias.
Propofol is not a substitute for lipid.
Expect a prolonged resuscitation; lipid plus CPR can take well over an hour, which is why bypass or ECMO are alerted early.

sections.heading: Afterwards
rows: At least 2 hours after a limited, rapidly resolving CNS event; at least 4–6 hours after a cardiovascular event, longer (24 hours is usual) after cardiac arrest
ASRA asks that events be reported to the LipidRescue registry (lipidrescue.org) and the institution's safety system
Lowest effective dose, incremental injection with aspiration, ultrasound guidance, a test dose where appropriate, and lipid available wherever significant doses are given
sections.note: ASRA states the 2020 checklist is current and under review, with an update expected in early 2027. Box wording here is a paraphrase; the ASRA PDF is the authority.

quickrefs.title: Malignant hyperthermia
quickrefs.society: Malignant Hyperthermia Association of the United States
quickrefs.summary: Stop the triggers, dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg at once and repeated, treat the potassium and the acidosis, cool to 38 °C — MHAUS's emergency treatment protocol and its post-crisis dantrolene recommendation, with the hotline number.

source.title: Emergency Treatment for an Acute MH Event (MHAUS)
source.citation: Malignant Hyperthermia Association of the United States. Managing a crisis: emergency treatment for an acute MH event; and Dantrolene administration after an MH event (2017). mhaus.org, accessed October 2026.

sections.heading: Recognize it
items: An unexplained rise in end-tidal CO₂ that outpaces ventilation is usually first; then tachycardia and tachypnea, masseter spasm or generalized rigidity, a mixed respiratory and metabolic acidosis, and rhabdomyolysis with myoglobinuria. Temperature can be a late sign.
Triggers are the volatile agents and succinylcholine; onset can be during the anesthetic or in the first hour or two of recovery.
MH hotline: 1-800-644-9737 (outside the United States 001-209-417-3722).

sections.heading: First minutes
items: Tell the surgeon; stop the volatile agent and succinylcholine; finish or abandon the surgery under a non-triggering intravenous anesthetic.
Call for help, the MH cart and dantrolene; in a surgicenter call 911; phone the hotline.

Hyperventilate with 100% oxygen at 10 L/min; put activated-charcoal filters on both limbs of the circuit if you have them (replace hourly); do not delay treatment to change the machine or the absorbent.

Dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV rapidly through a large-bore line; repeat until end-tidal CO₂ falls, rigidity eases and the heart rate settles — more than 10 mg/kg is sometimes needed; if large doses do nothing, reconsider the diagnosis.

Ryanodex 250 mg: add 5 mL sterile water and shake to an orange suspension. Dantrium or Revonto 20 mg: add 60 mL sterile water (no bacteriostatic agent) and shake until clear. Stock: 3 vials of Ryanodex or 36 of Dantrium/Revonto.
Send blood gases, potassium, CK, glucose, coagulation studies and urine myoglobin; place arterial and urinary catheters as the situation allows.

sections.heading: Treat what the muscle releases
rows: Hyperkalemia (K⁺ above 5.9 mmol/L, or lower with ECG changes)

Calcium chloride 10 mg/kg (maximum 2 g) or calcium gluconate 10–50 mg/kg (maximum 3 g); sodium bicarbonate 1–2 mEq/kg; insulin and glucose — adult 10 units regular insulin with 50 mL of 50% dextrose, child 0.1 units/kg with 2 mL/kg of 25% dextrose, glucose hourly; refractory: beta-agonist, dialysis, ECMO if in arrest
Sodium bicarbonate 1–2 mEq/kg when the base excess is more negative than −8, guided by blood gases
If CK or potassium is rising assume it: bicarbonate infusion about 1 mEq/kg/h to alkalinize the urine, diurese to more than 1 mL/kg/h (2 mL/kg/h once myoglobinuria is confirmed)
Cool when the core temperature passes 39 °C or climbs fast — cold intravenous saline, surface cooling, lavage; stop cooling at 38 °C to avoid overshoot
Treat conventionally after correcting potassium and acidosis; never a calcium channel blocker with dantrolene

sections.heading: After the crisis
rows: ICU for at least 24 hours with continuous temperature, capnography if intubated, ECG, oximetry and muscle tone; recrudescence can occur a day or more after the signs settle

1 mg/kg IV every 4–6 hours for at least 24 hours (an infusion of 0.25 mg/kg/h is the alternative); stretch the interval or stop only when all of: 24 hours of metabolic stability, core temperature below 38 °C, CK falling, no myoglobinuria, rigidity resolved
Blood gases, lactate and potassium every 8 hours; CK until it falls; creatinine daily if there was myoglobinuria
Report the event to the North American MH Registry, counsel the patient and family, and refer for muscle contracture or RYR1 genetic testing
sections.note: MHAUS's web protocol carries no revision date (site © 2026); the laminated poster sold by MHAUS follows the same protocol.

quickrefs.title: Preoperative fasting (ASA)
quickrefs.summary: The minimum fasting periods by substance for healthy patients having elective procedures, and what the 2023 update says about carbohydrate drinks, protein drinks, chewing gum and children's clear liquids.

source.title: 2023 American Society of Anesthesiologists Practice Guidelines for Preoperative Fasting: Carbohydrate-containing Clear Liquids with or without Protein, Chewing Gum, and Pediatric Fasting Duration — A Modular Update of the 2017 Practice Guidelines
source.citation: Joshi GP, Abdelmalak BB, Weigel WA, et al. Anesthesiology. 2023;138:132–151. doi:10.1097/ALN.0000000000004381 · Practice Guidelines for Preoperative Fasting and the Use of Pharmacologic Agents to Reduce the Risk of Pulmonary Aspiration. Anesthesiology. 2017;126:376–393.

sections.heading: Minimum fasting periods (2017, still in force)
rows: 2 hours — water, pulp-free fruit juice, carbonated drinks, clear tea, black coffee
6 hours (it empties like a solid; the amount matters)
sections.note: For healthy patients of all ages having elective procedures under general anesthesia, regional anesthesia or procedural sedation; not for women in labor. Meeting the times does not guarantee an empty stomach.

sections.heading: The 2023 update
rows: Healthy adults are encouraged to drink carbohydrate-containing clear liquids until 2 hours before; up to 400 mL is an appropriate volume (strong recommendation, moderate evidence). No separate recommendation for children
No recommendation to prefer them: the evidence is insufficient, and every drink studied also contained carbohydrate
Do not delay or cancel an elective procedure because a healthy adult chewed gum; remove the gum before any sedative or anesthetic; gum is not recommended as a preparation

A 1-hour limit was not endorsed and 2 hours was not re-graded: the task force found the evidence insufficient either way, and advises letting low-risk children drink clear liquids as close to 2 hours before as possible

sections.heading: When these times do not apply
sections.text: The guideline is written for healthy patients. Conditions that change gastric emptying or volume call for modified plans: pregnancy, obesity, diabetes, hiatal hernia and uncontrolled reflux, Zenker diverticulum, achalasia or stricture, previous gastric surgery, gastroparesis, opioid use, ileus or bowel obstruction or an acute intra-abdominal process, emergency procedures, enteral tube feeding, and patients with a potentially difficult airway. It does not cover procedures done without anesthesia or under local anesthesia alone.

quickrefs.title: Difficult airway: the ASA 2022 algorithm in brief
quickrefs.summary: The decision points of the 2022 ASA practice guideline: when to intubate awake, how to prepare, what to do after each failed attempt, the limit on attempts, the emergency invasive pathway, extubation, and what differs in children. A summary in Periop Signal's words; the ASA infographics are the algorithm.

source.title: 2022 American Society of Anesthesiologists Practice Guidelines for Management of the Difficult Airway
source.citation: Apfelbaum JL, Hagberg CA, Connis RT, et al. 2022 American Society of Anesthesiologists Practice Guidelines for Management of the Difficult Airway. Anesthesiology. 2022;136:31–81. doi:10.1097/ALN.0000000000004002

sections.heading: Before you start: five questions
items: Is laryngoscopy likely to be difficult? Assess several features (mouth opening, upper-lip bite test, Mallampati, thyromental distance, neck mobility) rather than any one; add bedside endoscopy or imaging when they would change the plan.
Is ventilation by face mask or supraglottic airway likely to be difficult?
Is the aspiration risk increased?
Will the patient desaturate quickly or not tolerate a brief apnea?
Would an emergency invasive airway be difficult (neck anatomy, prior surgery, radiation, obesity)?

sections.heading: Choose awake intubation when
sections.text: Difficult intubation is suspected and any one of the following holds: difficult mask or supraglottic ventilation, increased aspiration risk, intolerance of a brief apnea, or an expected difficult emergency invasive airway. When an awake technique is not feasible (an uncooperative patient, a child), intubate after induction with rescue options prepared. If the awake attempt fails and the case cannot wait or the patient is unstable, move to the post-induction pathway and prepare for an invasive airway.

sections.heading: Preparation
items: Standard equipment in the room and the portable difficult-airway unit immediately available; a second skilled clinician present or on call.
Tell the patient the risks; run a time-out that names the primary and backup airway managers and their roles; assign an observer to call out time, attempts and saturation so no one fixates.
Position, preoxygenate, and keep oxygen flowing throughout — including at extubation — with capnography to confirm ventilation.

sections.heading: After induction, attempt by attempt
items: Use the technique you know best first; if it struggles, combine devices (videolaryngoscope with a flexible scope, a supraglottic airway as a conduit).
Optimize before each try: position, relaxation, oxygenation (apneic oxygenation through the nose or a catheter).
After every attempt, provide and test mask ventilation when feasible, and decide: wake the patient and restore breathing, or carry on? Non-invasive or invasive next?
Limit attempts with any class of device to three, plus one more by a clinician with greater skill (3 + 1). Call for help early and use the algorithm as a cognitive aid.

sections.heading: Cannot intubate, cannot ventilate
items: Call for help; optimize oxygenation; try face mask, supraglottic airway and intubation as appropriate — treating functional obstruction (laryngospasm, light anesthesia) with drugs and anatomic obstruction with devices.

When non-invasive options have failed or are failing, go to an emergency invasive airway without further delay, by the most experienced person present, as fast as possible, with an alternative ready if it fails.

Techniques the guideline names: surgical cricothyrotomy, needle cricothyrotomy with a pressure-regulated jet device, large-bore cannula cricothyrotomy, surgical tracheostomy; rigid bronchoscopy in adults. The ASA does not name a single preferred technique; needle cricothyrotomy is reserved for age-appropriate children.
Start ECMO when appropriate and available.

sections.heading: Extubation
items: Have a formulated extubation and reintubation plan: readiness, the right time and place, a skilled person present.
Weigh awake extubation against extubation before return of consciousness, and whether an elective tracheostomy is wiser.

Consider a short-term airway exchange catheter or supraglottic airway to guide expedited reintubation (used sparingly in children); oxygen throughout; steroids or racemic epinephrine afterwards when indicated.
Document the difficulty and tell the patient — letter, alert bracelet, registry.

sections.heading: Children
sections.text: Awake intubation is uncommon; the usual path is inhalational induction with spontaneous ventilation maintained. Keep the anesthetic deep enough and reassess ventilation after every attempt; the three core tools are the supraglottic airway, the flexible scope and the videolaryngoscope, alone or combined. Separate functional from anatomic obstruction. The attempt limit is the primary manager's attempts (about three) plus one by the backup, then consider emerging the child and reversing drugs. Contact ECMO and ENT early when non-invasive failure is foreseeable; use airway exchange catheters with caution.

peds.note: Doses are from the FDA label, the AHA PALS algorithms (2020, re-checked against the October 2025 edition) and the Society for Pediatric Anesthesia's Pedi Crisis checklists; the source is on every line. Where the label gives no pediatric dose the line says so.

drugs.name: Propofol
drugs.note: Label: 3–16 years 2.5–3.5 mg/kg titrated to onset; adults 2–2.5 mg/kg; not labeled for induction under 3 years, where it is nonetheless the usual agent — titrate to effect. Maintenance 125–300 mcg/kg/min.
drugs.source: Diprivan FDA label, revised 2022

drugs.name: Ketamine
drugs.note: Label range 1–4.5 mg/kg over 60 seconds; 2 mg/kg gives 5–10 minutes of anesthesia. Pediatric use is off-label by the FDA wording.
drugs.source: Ketamine hydrochloride injection label (Pfizer), revised 2026

drugs.name: Ketamine
drugs.note: Label: 6.5–13 mg/kg; 9–13 mg/kg gives surgical anesthesia in 3–4 minutes lasting 12–25 minutes. Smaller doses are used for premedication; the label does not give them.
drugs.source: Ketamine hydrochloride injection label (Pfizer), revised 2026

drugs.name: Etomidate
drugs.note: Label: 0.2–0.6 mg/kg, usually 0.3 mg/kg over 30–60 seconds; not recommended under 10 years for lack of data.
drugs.source: Amidate prescribing information

drugs.name: Midazolam
drugs.note: Label: 6 months to 5 years 0.05–0.1 mg/kg initially, total up to 0.6 mg/kg (usually ≤ 6 mg); 6–12 years 0.025–0.05 mg/kg initially, total up to 0.4 mg/kg (usually ≤ 10 mg); 12–16 years adult dosing.
drugs.source: Midazolam hydrochloride injection label (Baxter)

drugs.name: Midazolam
drugs.note: Label: 0.25–0.5 mg/kg single dose from 6 months; younger or less cooperative children may need up to 1 mg/kg; maximum 20 mg.
drugs.source: Midazolam hydrochloride syrup label

drugs.name: Dexmedetomidine
drugs.note: Label (non-intubated children 1 month to under 18 years): 1.5 mcg/kg (1 month to under 2 years) or 2 mcg/kg (2 years and older) over 10 minutes, then 1.5 mcg/kg/h titrated 0.5–1.5 mcg/kg/h. Intraoperative bolus doses used in practice are smaller.
drugs.source: Precedex label, revised 2026

drugs.name: Succinylcholine
drugs.note: Label: 2 mg/kg for infants and small children, 1 mg/kg for older children and adolescents; boxed warning (hyperkalemic rhabdomyolysis in undiagnosed myopathy): reserve for emergency intubation or immediate airway control. Laryngospasm (Pedi Crisis): 0.1–2 mg/kg IV with atropine 0.02 mg/kg.
drugs.source: Succinylcholine chloride label; SPA Pedi Crisis 2025

drugs.name: Succinylcholine
drugs.note: Label: up to 3–4 mg/kg IM, total not more than 150 mg. Laryngospasm without access (Pedi Crisis): 2–4 mg/kg IM with atropine 0.04 mg/kg IM.
drugs.source: Succinylcholine chloride label; SPA Pedi Crisis 2025

drugs.name: Rocuronium
drugs.note: Label: 0.6 mg/kg intubating dose (0.45 mg/kg may suffice with sevoflurane), neonates to 17 years; 1.2 mg/kg is the adult rapid-sequence dose and the label does not recommend rocuronium for rapid sequence in children. Maintenance 0.075–0.125 mg/kg.
drugs.source: Rocuronium bromide label (DailyMed), revised 2019

drugs.name: Sugammadex
drugs.conc: 100 mg/mL; dilute to 10 mg/mL for small doses
drugs.note: Approved from 2 years of age at 2 and 4 mg/kg, on actual body weight; under 2 years not established.
drugs.source: Bridion FDA label, revised 2022

drugs.name: Sugammadex
drugs.note: Approved from 2 years of age.
drugs.source: Bridion FDA label, revised 2022

drugs.name: Sugammadex
drugs.note: Adult dose about 3 minutes after rocuronium; not studied in children, though the Pedi Crisis difficult-airway card lists it as rescue reversal.
drugs.source: Bridion FDA label, revised 2022; SPA Pedi Crisis 2025

drugs.name: Neostigmine
drugs.note: 0.03 mg/kg when two twitches are back or for shorter-acting agents; 0.07 mg/kg for deeper block or longer-acting agents; maximum 0.07 mg/kg or 5 mg. Give glycopyrrolate 0.2 mg per 1 mg of neostigmine.
drugs.source: Bloxiverz FDA label, revised 2023

drugs.name: Glycopyrrolate
drugs.note: Label: 4 mcg/kg, not more than 100 mcg per dose, repeated every 2–3 minutes as needed; premedication 4 mcg/kg IM 30–60 minutes before induction (infants under 2 years up to 9 mcg/kg). Reversal: 0.2 mg per 1 mg neostigmine.
drugs.source: Glycopyrrolate label (DailyMed), revised 2026

drugs.name: Epinephrine
drugs.note: 0.01 mg/kg, maximum 1 mg; give the first dose as early as possible for non-shockable rhythms. Endotracheal: 0.1 mg/kg of the 1 mg/mL strength.
drugs.source: AHA PALS 2020 (Topjian AA, et al. Circulation 2020;142:S469–S523) and the 2025 PALS algorithm text

drugs.name: Epinephrine
drugs.note: 0.01 mg/kg in the anterolateral thigh, maximum 0.3 mg under 30 kg and 0.5 mg at 30 kg or more, repeated every 5–15 minutes; IV 1–10 mcg/kg, infusion 0.02–1 mcg/kg/min, crystalloid 10–30 mL/kg (Pedi Crisis).
drugs.source: Adrenalin prescribing information 2022; SPA Pedi Crisis 2025

drugs.name: Atropine
drugs.note: 0.02 mg/kg, may repeat once; minimum 0.1 mg and maximum 0.5 mg per dose in the PALS bradycardia algorithm (1 mg from 12 years per the label). As premedication for emergency intubation PALS gives 0.02 mg/kg with no minimum.
drugs.source: AHA PALS 2020 (Topjian AA, et al. Circulation 2020;142:S469–S523) and the 2025 PALS algorithm text; atropine sulfate label

drugs.name: Amiodarone
drugs.note: 5 mg/kg bolus, up to 3 doses; the 2025 algorithm adds a 300 mg maximum first dose and 150 mg subsequently. With a pulse: 5 mg/kg over 20–60 minutes with expert advice. Lidocaine 1 mg/kg (maximum 100 mg) is the alternative in arrest.
drugs.source: AHA PALS 2020 (Topjian AA, et al. Circulation 2020;142:S469–S523) and the 2025 PALS algorithm text; SPA Pedi Crisis critical events checklists, January 2025 revision

drugs.name: Adenosine
drugs.note: Follow with a rapid flush; record the rhythm.
drugs.source: AHA PALS 2020 (Topjian AA, et al. Circulation 2020;142:S469–S523) and the 2025 PALS algorithm text

drugs.name: Adenosine
drugs.source: AHA PALS 2020 (Topjian AA, et al. Circulation 2020;142:S469–S523) and the 2025 PALS algorithm text

drugs.name: Defibrillation
drugs.note: Guideline text allows 2–4 J/kg for the first shock.
drugs.source: AHA PALS 2020 (Topjian AA, et al. Circulation 2020;142:S469–S523) and the 2025 PALS algorithm text

drugs.name: Defibrillation
drugs.note: Second shock 4 J/kg; later shocks 4 J/kg or more, to a maximum of 10 J/kg or the adult dose.
drugs.source: AHA PALS 2020 (Topjian AA, et al. Circulation 2020;142:S469–S523) and the 2025 PALS algorithm text

drugs.name: Synchronized cardioversion
drugs.note: Start at 0.5–1 J/kg; increase to 2 J/kg if ineffective; sedate when possible but do not delay.
drugs.source: AHA PALS 2020 (Topjian AA, et al. Circulation 2020;142:S469–S523) and the 2025 PALS algorithm text

drugs.name: Calcium chloride 10%
drugs.conc: 100 mg/mL (27 mg elemental calcium per mL); central or large vein
drugs.note: MHAUS: 10 mg/kg (maximum 2 g), or calcium gluconate 10–50 mg/kg (maximum 3 g); Pedi Crisis hyperkalemia 20 mg/kg. Routine calcium is not recommended in pediatric arrest without hyperkalemia, hypocalcemia, hypermagnesemia or calcium-channel-blocker overdose.
drugs.source: MHAUS; SPA Pedi Crisis critical events checklists, January 2025 revision; AHA PALS 2020 (Topjian AA, et al. Circulation 2020;142:S469–S523) and the 2025 PALS algorithm text

drugs.name: Sodium bicarbonate
drugs.note: Not routine in pediatric arrest except hyperkalemia or sodium-channel-blocker toxicity.
drugs.source: MHAUS; SPA Pedi Crisis critical events checklists, January 2025 revision; AHA PALS 2020 (Topjian AA, et al. Circulation 2020;142:S469–S523) and the 2025 PALS algorithm text

drugs.name: Dextrose
drugs.note: Pedi Crisis: D25 4 mL/kg under 2 years, 2 mL/kg from 2 years; the D25 label gives 0.25–0.5 g/kg (1–2 mL/kg) for infants, repeated as needed.
drugs.source: SPA Pedi Crisis critical events checklists, January 2025 revision; 25% dextrose injection label 2025

drugs.name: Dantrolene
drugs.conc: Ryanodex 250 mg in 5 mL; Dantrium or Revonto 20 mg in 60 mL
drugs.note: Repeat until end-tidal CO₂, rigidity and heart rate improve; more than 10 mg/kg is sometimes needed. Afterwards 1 mg/kg every 4–6 hours for at least 24 hours.
drugs.source: MHAUS emergency treatment protocol; Ryanodex label 2024

drugs.name: Lipid emulsion 20%
drugs.use: Local anesthetic toxicity, bolus over 1 min
drugs.note: Then 0.25 mL/kg/min; repeat the bolus every 3–5 minutes to 4.5 mL/kg; double the rate if pressure stays low; maximum 10 mL/kg over the first 30 minutes (Pedi Crisis). ASRA's adult regimen is in the LAST reference.
drugs.source: SPA Pedi Crisis critical events checklists, January 2025 revision

drugs.name: Naloxone
drugs.note: Label: 0.01 mg/kg initially, then 0.1 mg/kg if there is no response; for postoperative respiratory depression titrate 5–10 mcg increments every 2–3 minutes instead.
drugs.source: Naloxone hydrochloride injection prescribing information

drugs.name: Fentanyl
drugs.note: The label's pediatric statement (2–12 years) is a reduced dose 'as low as 2–3 mcg/kg' for induction and maintenance; 1–2 mcg/kg increments are the usual intraoperative analgesic dose.
drugs.source: Fentanyl citrate prescribing information; practice

drugs.name: Morphine
drugs.note: Titrated over 5–15 minutes (Pfizer label); IM or subcutaneous 0.1–0.2 mg/kg (maximum 15 mg) every 4–6 hours; neonatal safety not established.
drugs.source: Morphine sulfate injection label (Pfizer)

drugs.name: Hydromorphone
drugs.conc: 0.2 to 2 mg/mL syringes — check the strength
drugs.note: Off-label in children: the label states safety and effectiveness in pediatric patients are not established; 10–15 mcg/kg is common practice and should be confirmed against your formulary.
drugs.source: Hydromorphone hydrochloride injection label (Pfizer), revised 2026; institutional practice

drugs.name: Acetaminophen
drugs.note: 2–12 years and adolescents under 50 kg: 15 mg/kg every 6 hours or 12.5 mg/kg every 4 hours, maximum 75 mg/kg/day; 29 days to 2 years 15 mg/kg every 6 hours (60 mg/kg/day); neonates 12.5 mg/kg every 6 hours (50 mg/kg/day); 50 kg and over 1 g every 6 hours.
drugs.source: Ofirmev prescribing information, revised 2018

drugs.name: Ibuprofen
drugs.conc: dilute to 4 mg/mL or less; over at least 10 minutes
drugs.note: 6 months to under 12 years: 10 mg/kg to a maximum single dose of 400 mg; daily maximum 40 mg/kg or 2.4 g; 12–17 years 400 mg.
drugs.source: Caldolor FDA label, revised 2021

drugs.name: Ketorolac
drugs.note: Off-label: the label says ketorolac is not indicated in pediatric patients (only single-dose pharmacokinetics at 0.5 mg/kg); 0.5 mg/kg to a maximum of 30 mg is the practice adopted here.
drugs.source: Ketorolac tromethamine injection label, revised 2020; institutional practice

drugs.name: Ondansetron
drugs.note: Label: 1 month to 12 years, 0.1 mg/kg up to 40 kg and 4 mg above 40 kg, over 2–5 minutes. The PONV consensus gives 0.05–0.1 mg/kg (maximum 4 mg).
drugs.source: Ondansetron injection label; Fourth PONV consensus, Table 6

drugs.name: Dexamethasone
drugs.note: 0.15 mg/kg, maximum 5 mg, from the consensus pediatric table (the FDA label gives no PONV dose).
drugs.source: Fourth PONV consensus (Gan TJ, et al. Anesth Analg 2020), Table 6

drugs.name: Cefazolin
drugs.use: Surgical prophylaxis, within 60 min of incision
drugs.note: 30 mg/kg to a maximum of 2 g (3 g from 120 kg in adults), redosed every 4 hours of surgery, per the ASHP/IDSA/SIS/SHEA 2013 guideline as reproduced in open sources; follow your institution's antimicrobial protocol.
drugs.source: Bratzler DW, et al. Am J Health Syst Pharm 2013;70:195–283 (via secondary sources)

localAnesthetics.name: Bupivacaine
localAnesthetics.note: Single injection; infusions 0.4 mg/kg/h (0.2 mg/kg/h under 6 months).
localAnesthetics.source: ASRA/ESRA pediatric regional anesthesia recommendations 2018 (Suresh S, et al. Reg Anesth Pain Med 2018;43:211–216), as reproduced in open appraisals

localAnesthetics.name: Ropivacaine
localAnesthetics.note: Single injection; 2 mg/kg is the cited maximum for a caudal.

localAnesthetics.name: Lidocaine
localAnesthetics.note: 7 mg/kg with epinephrine. Widely cited maximum; confirm against your reference before relying on it.
localAnesthetics.source: Standard references (not verified from the ASRA/ESRA text in this review)
